Certain principles of management are, however, well es- tablished. • monotherapy is preferable to a multiple-drug regimen and treatment is therefore begun with a single drug, in- creasing the dose gradually until seizures are brought under control or adverse effects become unacceptable • if treatment with the first drug fails, it is preferable to try alternative single first-line antiepileptics before giving combinations of drugs. It has been suggested that for practical purposes a patient should be considered to have refractory epilepsy if seizure control is not ob- tained with consecutive trials of 2 well tolerated antiepileptics26 • the change-over from one antiepileptic to another should be made cautiously, withdrawing the first drug only when the new regimen has been largely established • if combinations are necessary in intractable cases, regi- mens should avoid the inclusion, where possible, of se- dating drugs such as the barbiturates or benzodiazepines • drugs with different modes of action should be selected for combined therapy, to reduce the risk that adverse ef- fects will be additive • many antiepileptics interact with each other through complex mechanisms and dosage adjustments may be necessary to maintain plasma concentrations within the therapeutic range; plasma monitoring may be advisable with combination therapy. (UK guidelines16 recom- mend regular monitoring of antiepileptic drug concen- trations only when clinically indicated, e.g. to manage pharmacokinetic interactions, or in cases of suspected toxicity or non-adherence) • if trials of combination therapy do not produce worth- while benefits, treatment should revert to the regimen (monotherapy or combination) that has provided the most acceptable balance of seizure control and adverse effects Around 60% of patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy will respond to monotherapy with the first- or second- choice antiepileptic without developing intolerable ad- verse effects. The remaining 30 to 40% will have epilepsy that is difficult to control from the start, although some of these patients will respond to combination therapy.26 Pa- tients who fail to respond to adequate medical treatment may be considered for resective surgery; vagus nerve stim- ulation by means of an implanted device has also proved effective in those with severe intractable epilepsy who ex- perience an aura before the onset of a seizure.17,18 UK guidelines recommend consideration of the adjunctive use of vagus nerve stimulation in patients refractory to drug therapy but unsuitable for resective surgery.15,16 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed 466 Antiepileptics Partial seizures with or without secondary generalisa- tion may be treated with carbamazepine or valproate, or with the newer drugs lamotrigine or oxcarbazepine.15,16,29 Topiramate is also used, as monotherapy or as an adjunct to other treatments (in the UK, it is considered a first
